newsitem.title: USA: GM to begin making longer-range electric vehicle.
newsitem.headline: GM to begin making longer-range electric vehicle.

text.p: General Motors Corp. later this year will begin producing a new battery for its EV1 electric car that will double the range of the rounded coupe to up to 140 miles, the head of GM's advanced technology unit said Thursday.

Retail buyers who want to lease the longer-range electric car, which comes with a nickel-metal hydride battery, will be able to do so sometime in calendar 1998, said Robert Purcell, executive director of GM's advanced technology vehicles.

"As we put the advanced batteries in the car, we're going to absolutely set the range benchmark for any electric vehicle," said Purcell, who spoke at a press briefing at the University of Michigan's annual automotive conference here.
Owners will typically be able to get combined highway and city driving range of 120 to 140 miles on a single charge, Purcell said.
The only other electrically powered car now offered to retail buyers is the EV Plus, which Honda Motor Co. Ltd. started selling in California in April.
The EV Plus also uses the more efficient nickel-metal hydride battery, but it is a heavier vehicle that seats four people. Honda said it has a "real world" driving range of 60 to 80 miles.

The nickel-metal hydride batteries on the EV1 will be sold as an option and will cost more than cars with the older lead acid batteries. GM, which loses money on each EV1 it sells, has not determined how much it will subsidise the new batteries, Purcell said.

Eight months after GM became the first major automaker to start selling an electric car, it has leased about 215 of the vehicles. In addition, the automaker has sold approximately 200 S-10 electric compact pickup trucks.

Despite the small numbers, Purcell said GM considers its electric vehicle programme a success. Customer feedback for the EV1 indicates the car has become an integral part of owners' daily driving routine, he said.
"They're driving the car every day," Purcell said. "It has become the primary use car."
Purcell declined to reveal GM's internal volume projections, saying the success of the vehicle cannot be measured after eight months of sales.

Slow sales prompted GM to cut the EV1's lease price earlier this year. Including government financial credits, buyers in southern California can lease an EV1 for $399 a month, down from the previous $475 monthly payment. That figure does not cover the charger installation, which costs $800 to $1,000.
Looking ahead, GM plans to revise the EV1's drive systems and electronic components every two to three years to lower costs and improve performance, Purcell said.

By the time the third-generation EV1 is developed four to six years from now, he said, GM aims to bring down the cost of the vehicle's drive train and electronic components to about the same level as a traditional internal combustion engine.
